clue.text: A British employer, one who uses bad language

parts.note: an employer here is literally one who employs, that is uses, something

explanation.surface: A British boss is accused of swearing at staff.
explanation.walkthrough: 'employer' looks like a boss but is read as 'one who employs', giving USER.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who hurls abuse, especially verbal insults, uses bad language at people.

clue.text: Cove in France where sluggish tributary appears

parts.note: a cove is a small bay
ou is the French word for where

explanation.surface: A cove somewhere in France is where a slow stream enters the sea.
explanation.definitionFit: A bayou is a slow-moving marshy outlet or offshoot of a river, as in Louisiana.

clue.text: Using force, do powerful damage in East End

parts.note: powerful means strong

indicators.note: East End Cockney speech drops the initial H, so the word for damage loses it

parts.note: to damage is to harm

explanation.surface: A thug uses violence to cause serious damage in London's East End.
explanation.walkthrough: The East End of London is famous for Cockney speech, which drops initial H sounds; 'do' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: Strong-arm tactics are those that rely on force or threats of violence.

clue.text: Be left to see about the power supply

parts.note: re means about or concerning
the mains, or main, is the electricity supply

explanation.surface: Someone stays behind to check on the electricity supply.
explanation.definitionFit: To remain is to stay behind or be left over when others have gone.

clue.text: Break the rules to get popular kind of benefit

parts.note: in means fashionable or popular
a fringe benefit is a perk given alongside wages

explanation.surface: A worker bends the rules to obtain a perk.
explanation.definitionFit: To infringe a rule or law is to violate or break it.

clue.text: Having nothing on late tonight here, perhaps

definitions.text: Having nothing on late tonight here, perhaps

parts.words: Having nothing on late tonight here, perhaps
parts.note: reads like a TV listing with no programmes scheduled late at night, but means being completely unclothed

explanation.surface: A schedule shows nothing on late tonight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Having nothing on' suggests an empty diary or schedule; really it means wearing no clothes.
explanation.definitionFit: The altogether is an idiom for nakedness, so this phrase means wearing no clothes at all.

clue.text: Combustible mixture sparked off by a redcap

parts.note: sparked off means fired, as an engine or gun is fired
a redcap is a British military policeman, abbreviated MP

explanation.surface: An explosive mix is ignited by a military policeman.
explanation.walkthrough: Redcap is British slang for a military policeman, from the red cap band; 'by' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: Firedamp is the explosive methane-air mixture that builds up in coal mines.

clue.text: Religion I criticise severely

parts.note: to slam is to criticise harshly

explanation.surface: Someone confesses to harshly attacking a faith.
explanation.definitionFit: Islam is the monotheistic faith founded by the prophet Muhammad.

clue.text: Dregs the Spanish feed to the birds

parts.note: grounds are the dregs left at the bottom of a coffee cup
el is the Spanish word for the

explanation.surface: Someone tips coffee dregs out for the birds in Spain.
explanation.definitionFit: Groundsel is a common weed whose seeds are traditionally fed to caged birds.

clue.text: One testing water in sound a short distance past hotel

indicators.note: past means coming after, so this piece follows the hotel

parts.note: a hydro is a spa hotel offering water treatments

indicators.note: in sound tells us the word for a short distance is to be taken by how it is spoken

parts.note: a metre is a short distance

explanation.surface: Someone tests the water in a sound just past a hotel.
explanation.walkthrough: Hydro is a British term for a spa hotel; METRE said out loud is METER, the spelling the answer needs.
explanation.definitionFit: A hydrometer measures the density of liquids such as water.

clue.text: Computer subroutine taking Kitty aback

indicators.note: aback means backwards, so the word for kitty is read in reverse

parts.note: a kitty is a pool of shared money

explanation.surface: A programmer's routine catches the cat off guard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Kitty' looks like a cat but is a fund of money, a POOL; 'taking' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: A loop is a sequence of program instructions that repeats, a basic computing routine.

clue.text: Go to top of hill by old road

parts.note: a go, as in a game, is a turn
a pike is a pointed hilltop, especially in the Lake District

explanation.surface: Someone climbs to the summit beside an ancient track.
explanation.walkthrough: Pike is a northern English word for a peaked hill; 'by' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: A turnpike was a historic toll road with a gate where travellers paid.

clue.text: Peremptory request from damned crook

indicators.note: crook here means bent or twisted, so the letters of damned are reshaped

explanation.surface: A cursed criminal makes a curt request.
explanation.walkthrough: 'crook' looks like a criminal, but is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A demand is a forceful request that brooks no refusal.

clue.text: Paediatrician restraining recurrent wheeze

indicators.note: recurrent means running back, so the held letters read backwards
restraining means holding within, so the letters sit inside Paediatrician

explanation.surface: A children's doctor treats a recurring wheezy chest.
explanation.walkthrough: AEDI sits inside Paediatrician and reads backwards as the answer; 'wheeze' looks medical but means a clever scheme.
explanation.definitionFit: In British English a wheeze is a clever plan or scheme, that is a notion.

clue.text: A mad Latin sort of dog

indicators.note: sort here is a verb, to rearrange, so these letters are sorted into a new order

explanation.surface: A crazy Latin-speaking hound of some kind.
explanation.definitionFit: A Dalmatian is a breed of spotted dog from the Croatian coast.

clue.text: Movingly, top psalm can provide a pillar of light

indicators.note: movingly signals the letters of top psalm being moved around

explanation.surface: A stirring hymn lights up the congregation like a beacon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Movingly' looks like emotional praise of the psalm; it is the anagram signal. 'can provide' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A lamp post is a tall column carrying a street light.

clue.text: Pan imitation fabric

parts.note: Peter Pan is the boy who never grew up
a sham is an imitation or fake

explanation.surface: A fake Peter Pan costume is made of cloth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pan' looks like a cooking vessel but stands for PETER, as in Peter Pan.
explanation.definitionFit: Petersham is a heavy ribbed cotton or silk ribbon fabric used for hatbands and waistbands.

clue.text: One may take a quick snap here

definitions.text: One may take a quick snap here

parts.words: One may take a quick snap here
parts.note: sounds like a photographer's spot, but snap is a hasty bite to eat

explanation.surface: A place to take a quick photograph.
explanation.walkthrough: 'snap' suggests a photograph; in northern English it is a packed lunch or quick bite.
explanation.definitionFit: A snack bar is a counter selling quick light meals.

clue.text: Angry love-bird

parts.note: flaming means furious, angry
love is zero in tennis, written as the letter O

explanation.surface: A lovebird is in a temper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'love-bird' reads as one word, but splits into O and the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The flamingo is a pink long-legged wading bird.

clue.text: Hat rejected by most of the best people

indicators.note: rejected means sent back, so the word is read backwards
most of means the word loses its last letter

parts.note: the elite are the best people in a group

explanation.surface: A hat is spurned by most of high society.
explanation.walkthrough: ELITE loses its last letter to give ELIT, which is then turned round.
explanation.definitionFit: Tile is old slang for a hat, especially a top hat.

clue.text: 25 in a note raised for a mackintosh, for instance

indicators.note: in places one piece inside the other
raised in a down clue means turned upwards, so the note is reversed

parts.note: me (or mi) is a note in the sol-fa scale
a pony is British slang for twenty-five pounds

explanation.surface: Twenty-five pounds goes on a coat in a note.
explanation.walkthrough: '25' points to a slang sum of money, not to another clue; in a down clue 'raised' means read upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: The mackintosh raincoat is named after its inventor Charles Macintosh, so it is a word named after a person.

clue.text: Resin in wine swallowed by master of ceremonies

indicators.note: swallowed by means taken inside, so the wine goes inside the host's letters

parts.note: Asti is an Italian sparkling wine

explanation.surface: A host gulps down wine with resin in it.
explanation.definitionFit: Mastic is an aromatic gum from the mastic tree, used in varnish.

clue.text: Secure business association

definitions.meaning: to fasten or tie something firmly
a link or merger between companies

explanation.definitionFit: A tie-up is both a fastening and a commercial link between firms.

clue.text: Fire in eastern island, and in the heavens

indicators.note: in places the fire inside the island

parts.note: Man is the Isle of Man
a pyre is a fire for burning a body

explanation.surface: A funeral fire burns on an eastern island and rises skywards.
explanation.definitionFit: Empyrean means of the highest heaven, celestial.

clue.text: Not the first nurse said to carry a gun

indicators.note: not the first means the opening letter is dropped from the word for nurse
said tells us the word for nurse is taken as spoken and spelt another way with the same sound

parts.note: a nurse for children is a nanny

explanation.surface: A nurse says she is no novice at handling firearms.
explanation.walkthrough: NANNY spoken can be spelt NANNIE; dropping its first letter leaves the name. The definition alludes to the musical Annie Get Your Gun, about the sharpshooter Annie Oakley.
explanation.definitionFit: The title character of the musical Annie Get Your Gun is told to carry a firearm.

clue.text: Source of honey I possess?

indicators.note: source means start, so the first letter of honey is taken

parts.note: I possess is I have, contracted to I've

explanation.surface: A beekeeper wonders whether they own a supply of honey.
explanation.definitionFit: Bees make honey in a hive, so it is the source of the honey a keeper possesses.

clue.text: Late, following ovation

parts.note: following means coming behind
a hand is a round of applause

explanation.surface: Applause comes late after the show.
explanation.definitionFit: Behindhand means late or in arrears.

clue.text: Motivator fiddling rise in PR

indicators.note: fiddling with something alters it, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A public relations man cooks the books to boost profits.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' is part of the pool, not a container signal.
explanation.definitionFit: An inspirer is someone who motivates others.

clue.text: As an example, arm someone with a club

definitions.meaning: an arm is an example of a limb
a person belonging to a society or club

explanation.definitionFit: A member is both a limb and someone who belongs to a club.
